A.explanation: This divides the $200g$ resultant force by the old $3200\text{ kg}$ mass instead of the new $3000\text{ kg}$ mass.

B.explanation: The resultant upward force is $200 \times 9.81\text{ N}$ and dividing by the new mass $3000\text{ kg}$ gives $0.654\text{ m s}^{-2}$ upwards.

C.explanation: This is $g$ alone and ignores that upthrust still supports almost all of the weight, leaving only a small resultant force.

D.explanation: This divides the full unchanged upthrust $3200g$ by $3000\text{ kg}$ without subtracting the new weight $3000g$.

hints: Notice the submarine is first at rest, so the unchanged upthrust must equal the initial weight of the $3200\text{ kg}$ mass.
After $200\text{ kg}$ of water is pumped out horizontally, the upward force exceeds the new downward weight by the weight of that $200\text{ kg}$.
Calculate the net upward force as $200 \times 9.81\text{ N}$ and then use $F = ma$ with the new total mass of $3000\text{ kg}$.
walkthrough: Initially at rest vertically, resultant force is zero, so upthrust $U$ equals initial weight: $U = 3200 \times 9.81\text{ N}$.
After pumping, total mass is $3200 - 200 = 3000\text{ kg}$, so new weight is $W = 3000 \times 9.81\text{ N}$ while $U$ is unchanged.
The initial upward resultant force is $F = U - W = (3200 - 3000) \times 9.81 = 200 \times 9.81\text{ N} = 1962\text{ N}$.
Use Newton's second law with the moving mass: $a = F/m = 1962 / 3000$ with units $\text{m s}^{-2}$.
This gives $a = 0.654\text{ m s}^{-2}$ upwards. This is option B.
